feedback: If sunlight still lands on the spot: 'Is your spot still in a bright patch of sunlight? Move your cover until your spot is in its shadow — shade is wherever the light is blocked.'
If the child declares success without comparing: 'How do you know it's cooler? Let's check a covered spot and a sunny spot side by side at the same time and feel/measure both.'

If a see-through or thin cover is used: 'Put each cover over the spot and look at the GROUND — which one still shows a bright patch, and which casts a dark shadow? Then test which cover keeps the spot coolest compared with a sunny spot. (Never look up at the sun through the cover.)'

If the build is treated as finished after one try: 'Change just one thing — maybe make it bigger or use a thicker cloth — and test again, comparing the shaded and sunny spots to see if it gets cooler.'
activities.intendedInsight: A shade works by getting between the sun and the area and blocking the sunlight; you can tell it worked because the shaded spot is cooler than a matching sunny spot checked at the same time, not because it looks nice.
learnerActions: Start from a real problem the child cares about: 'the slide / sandpit / our toy gets too hot in the sun — can you build something to keep it cool?'

Offer a kit — cloths, card, sticks, pegs — and ask the child to choose a material and build a cover (umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol) over a target spot (a thermometer, a toy, or something to keep cool such as a chocolate or ice cube on the ground).
Have the child place the cover so it sits BETWEEN the sun and the spot; look at the ground and move the cover until the target spot is in the cover's shadow instead of bright sunlight.

Set up a fair comparison: two of the same kind of spot that start out alike, one shaded by the structure and one left in the sun, then check both after the same time has passed, by careful feel or with a relative thermometer.
Improve one thing and re-test (bigger? thicker/more opaque? angled to block the sun's path?), then judge success from the evidence: is the shaded spot cooler than the sunny one?
activities.title: Build, position and test a real shade

feedback: If the see-through cover is chosen as coolest: 'Look at the ground under each cover — the sun still makes a bright patch under the see-through one. Which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground?'
If correct: 'Yes — that cover blocks the sun and casts a dark shadow, so the spot stays cooler.'
activities.intendedInsight: A solid, well-positioned cover casts a dark shadow and keeps the spot cooler than a see-through or poorly placed one.
learnerActions: Pose a picture + audio question such as 'which shade keeps it coolest?' or 'is the spot under the umbrella warmer or cooler?' comparing a see-through cover with a solid one.
Ask the child to match a shade structure to the cooler shaded area beneath it, looking at which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground.
Keep temperature language relative (warmer/cooler) and provide adult/audio support for pre-readers.
activities.title: Quick check — which cover keeps it coolest? (recognition)
